#### *94–2 vote cements former rival’s place in Obama’s ‘Team of Rivals’ cabinet following brief GOP ethics debate.*

**WASHINGTON** — The Senate voted overwhelmingly on Wednesday to confirm Hillary Rodham Clinton as the nation’s 67th Secretary of State, clearing the way for the former First Lady and New York senator to take the helm of American diplomacy under President Barack Obama.

The 94-to-2 vote came just one day after President Obama’s inauguration, following a brief delay staged by Senate Republicans over potential conflicts of interest stemming from former President Bill Clinton’s international charitable foundation.

Mrs. Clinton, 61, is expected to resign her Senate seat immediately and be sworn in later today at the State Department, ending her eight-year tenure representing New York and completing a remarkable political arc from Mr. Obama’s fiercest primary competitor to his chief foreign policy envoy.

John Kerry (D-Mass.), chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, speaking on the Senate floor shortly before the vote. "She has the stature, the intellect, and the stamina to hit the ground running."

### **Ethics Debate and a Roll-Call Delay**

Democrats had hoped to confirm Mrs. Clinton by unanimous consent on Tuesday shortly after Mr. Obama took the oath of office. However, Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) objected, forcing Wednesday’s formal roll-call vote. 

While Mr. Cornyn ultimately voted in favor of confirmation, he insisted on a public debate regarding the financial transparency of the William J. Clinton Foundation. Republicans raised concerns that foreign governments seeking influence with the Obama administration might attempt to curry favor through massive donations to the former president’s global initiatives.

To satisfy congressional concerns, the foundation agreed to publish the names of its donors annually and restrict fundraising from foreign nations while Mrs. Clinton serves as Secretary of State. 

"The American people deserve to know that the foreign policy of the United States is unencumbered by any potential or perceived conflict of interest," Mr. Cornyn said during floor debate. "I believe the steps taken are a good faith effort, but the Senate must remain vigilant."

Only two senators voted against Mrs. Clinton’s confirmation: Sen. Jim DeMint (R-S.C.) and Sen. David Vitter (R-La.). Mr. DeMint cited concerns that Mrs. Clinton’s foreign policy view was overly reliant on international institutions at the expense of American sovereignty.

### **A Shift to "Smart Power"**

During her confirmation hearings before the Foreign Relations Committee last week, Mrs. Clinton outlined a stark departure from the unilateral approach that critics associated with the early years of the Bush administration. She pledged to deploy "smart power"—a doctrine combining military, diplomatic, economic, political, and cultural tools.

"We must use what has been called 'smart power'—the full range of tools at our disposal," Mrs. Clinton testified last Tuesday. "With the right inputs, diplomacy is hard-headed, clear-eyed, and pragmatic."

Among her immediate challenges will be managing the troop drawdown in Iraq, addressing the deteriorating security situation in Afghanistan, confronting Iran’s nuclear ambitions, and navigating the ongoing economic crisis, which has weakened global markets.

### **Farewell to New York**

The confirmation marks the end of Mrs. Clinton’s tenure in the Senate, where she has served since 2001 after carving out an independent political career following her time as First Lady. 

Her departure leaves a vacancy in New York’s congressional delegation, placing the spotlight on New York Governor David Paterson. Under state law, Gov. Paterson holds the sole authority to appoint a replacement to serve until a special election in November 2010. Contenders reportedly being considered for the seat include Rep. Kirsten Gillibrand, Rep. Carolyn Maloney, and Caroline Kennedy, daughter of the late President John F. Kennedy.

In a emotional statement released following the vote, Mrs. Clinton expressed gratitude to her constituents. 

"Serving the people of New York has been the honor of my life," she said. "While I am stepping down from the Senate, I am not stepping away from service to our nation, and I will carry the spirit and resilience of New Yorkers with me around the globe."
